title: Do RSI, MACD and other indicators predict returns?
author: MehmetSaruhan
selftext:
**The short answer**  
Only weakly — and mostly the opposite way to how they are usually read. Over the next week, US stocks with RSI(14) below 30 beat the median stock 51.6% of the time and those above 70 only 48.5%; a close above the upper Bollinger band 48.6%, a new 10-day high 48.7%. That is short-run reversal, not momentum. MACD and golden crosses showed no reliable edge.  
  
**How this was measured**  
Every Wednesday since 1995, the stocks in our universe are compared on the signal and followed for 1, 5, 21 and 63 trading sessions. A reading counts when the stock beat the median stock on the same day, so chance is always 50 in 100 and a market-wide rally cannot flatter the result. The strength of a relation is a rank correlation (IC) between the signal and the forward return; its t-statistic is taken on non-overlapping dates, and a relation is called proven only when |t| is at least 3, it held in at least 60% of years and it is large enough to matter. With hundreds of tests, a looser bar would pass about one in twenty by luck. Studies run Sep 24, 2026; outcomes measured through Aug 21, 2026.  
  
For the rest of research:  
[**https://opulencealpha.ai/studies/technical-indicators**](https://opulencealpha.ai/studies/technical-indicators)

comments.author: profittoinvest
comments.body:
RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands, moving averages etc. are useful tools, but none of them gives you an edge just because you put it on a chart.

I’d approach it more like an experiment.

Start with a very simple entry rule based on one indicator and test it. First 10 trades are only a sanity check — not proof of anything. Then look for additional information that helps filter the bad entries: volatility, trend regime, momentum, volume, market structure, whatever actually improves the results.

Then repeat the process:

10 trades → 100 trades → 1,000 trades.

Test, measure, change one thing at a time, test again.

And don’t focus only on win rate. A strategy with a 40% win rate can be much better than one with 70% if the winners are significantly larger than the losers.

The real question is not “does RSI predict returns?” but:

**Can I define a repeatable set of conditions where the combination of entry, exit and risk management produces positive expectancy over a large sample?**

That’s where the edge starts to appear.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
I agree with the framing, and one caution on the loop: "change one thing at a time and test again" on the same data is how a filter set slowly gets fitted to history. Each tweak is another trial, so I'd keep a count of how many variations you've tried, and reserve a final period you don't touch until the rules are frozen. Also, 1,000 trades from a single regime can still mislead, so it helps to see the result across a trend, a range and a sharp selloff.

The study in the post is a useful reminder of the scale involved. A 51.6% versus 48.5% hit rate for oversold versus overbought is a tiny edge, small enough that costs and slippage could erase it for an active strategy. Your expectancy point is exactly why that matters: what counts is the average win, average loss and trading costs together, not just the direction.

For the "additional information" step, event context is a good filter to test, meaning whether a trade fires near CPI, FOMC or earnings. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing for that.

replies.author: profittoinvest
replies.body:
Good point — I agree. “Change one thing at a time” can still lead to overfitting if you keep optimizing on the same historical sample.

That’s why I’d separate research from validation: use one period to develop the rules, then freeze them and test them on data you didn’t optimize against. And after that, compare the frozen model with LIVE execution.

I also agree that 1,000 trades from one market regime can still be misleading. A strategy should survive different environments — trend, range, high volatility, low volatility and sharp selloffs.

In our own work, that LIVE vs backtest comparison has probably been the most useful part, because it shows where the model looks good on paper but behaves differently in real execution.

And yes — expectancy after costs matters much more than raw hit rate.

replies.author: MehmetSaruhan
replies.body: Actually, our platform is an AI/ML investment platform where we use these indicators as features. While some provide direct alpha (Information Coefficient) and others offer broader context, we ultimately feed about 1,700 features into our model families. We publish these findings to encourage technical traders to explore our research: [https://opulencealpha.ai/studies/](https://opulencealpha.ai/studies/)

replies.author: profittoinvest
replies.body: Interesting approach. 1,700 features is quite a large feature space — I’d be especially curious how you control for overfitting and feature redundancy over time.
